newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Sporadic shooting in Zaire's capital Kinshasa.
newsitem.headline: Sporadic shooting in Zaire's capital Kinshasa.

text.p: Sporadic automatic weapons fire crackled in different parts of Zaire's capital Kinshasa on Saturday after rebels said their troops were entering the city, but it was not clear who was firing on whom.
A sustained small-arms firefight was going on in the main market area involving men in military uniform as well as civilian dress, a Reuters Television crew said.

"We can see men running in and out of a house in an alley collecting weapons including rocket-propelled grenade launchers," an RTV producer said from the roof of a seven-storey hotel. "There's been pretty steady firing."
Several thousand metres (yards) away, sporadic automatic weapons fire and two short bursts of heavy machinegun fire could be heard at about 7 a.m. (0600 GMT) and scattered shots later.
There was no indication of intensive fighting involving artillery, mortars or tanks.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said his forces were already marching into the capital from the direction of the airport which lies about 15 km (10 miles) east of the city.
People on the airport road, which was largely deserted, told a Reuters photographer they had seen armoured vehicles of the Zairean army moving towards town.

As dawn broke over Kinshasa on Saturday, its five million people waited anxiously to see if there would be a fight for the final prize in Zaire's seven-month civil war, or if the army would join Kabila's revolution.
International mediators who worked for a peaceful transition in the huge Central African republic had sought a "soft landing" for the capital. But it was unlikely to be entirely bloodless.

Hours after President Mobutu Sese Seko's exit and abdication from power, army chief of staff and defence minister General Mahele Lieko Bokungu was shot dead at Camp Tshatshi presidential barracks, apparently while trying to restore order among members of Mobutu's elite presidential guard.
His killing raised the spectre of a power vacuum that could lead to a settling of scores by Mobutu loyalists who believe top regular army officers betrayed the presidency.
At one point, armoured vehicles were brought to an international hotel where senior officers and their families had taken refuge during the night, and guests were advised to stay in their rooms.
The vehicles left before first light and there was no clear indication whether anyone had been removed from the hotel.

A government spokesman, announcing in a studiously oblique statement that Mobutu was giving up power, assured the people on Friday that Kinshasa would be protected and defended "in order to avert bloodshed".
It was not clear whether this meant the army would resist the advancing enemy.
Many in Kinshasa were preparing to welcome Kabila's soldiers, but as of Saturday morning it seemed they were still waiting.
